query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the powder mass feed rate during the thermal‐spray deposition will build up a thicker FeCoNiCrAl bond coat while not increasing in‐flight oxidation, thereby preserving the desired coating integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high‐entropy alloy powder with particle sizes of 15–45 μm used under conventional thermal-spray conditions which currently yield insufficient deposit thickness.
generation.intervention: Increase the powder feed rate (i.e., deliver a higher mass flow of feedstock) during the spray process while keeping other parameters (e.g., carrier gas composition, spray distance) constant.
generation.conditions: Use atmospheric plasma spraying parameters optimized for bond coat deposition in thermal barrier systems; maintain an inert atmosphere with controlled spray distance such that in-flight heating and oxidation remain minimal.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced splat overlap and a denser, more continuous deposit due to higher material delivery, promoting rapid layer build-up without extended particle dwell times that encourage oxidation.
generation.mechanism: Delivering more feedstock per unit time increases the deposition rate so that thicker layers are built up in fewer passes. The reduced exposure time of individual particles to the high-temperature flame minimizes the oxidation extent, thereby retaining coating integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The bond coat will exceed the baseline thickness (15–45 μm) achieving the required coating thickness for TBC systems, while the microstructure remains intact and the level of as-sprayed oxidation remains comparable to the standard process.
generation.baseline: Coatings deposited using the original feed rate with 15–45 μm feedstock, which result in insufficient layer thickness.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective as long as the increased feed rate does not lead to particle agglomeration, poor splat formation, or excessive thermal loading. It assumes that plasma power, gas flows, and spray distance are held constant and optimized to limit oxidation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise multiplier for the feed rate increase required to achieve target thickness without compromising microstructural quality is not defined and may need further experimental calibration. There is also some uncertainty whether too high a feed rate might lead to splashing or uneven coatings.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings on identical substrates under otherwise constant atmospheric plasma spray conditions. One set is produced with the standard feed rate and the other with an increased feed rate. Ensure the spray distance, gas composition, and plasma power remain unchanged. Compare the thickness, oxidation level, and microstructural features of the resulting coatings.
measurements: Oxidation level and phase composition via XRD and EDS analysis
Microstructural integrity (e.g., splat morphology) via SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the increased feed rate does not produce a statistically significant increase in coating thickness or, alternatively, if it leads to a measurable increase in oxidation (e.g., higher oxide phase content) or microstructural degradation compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

For example, both as-cast AlSiTiCrFeCoNiMo0.5 and AlSiTiCrFeNiMo0.5 are dual-phase alloys (BCC + FCC); however, if fabricated via thermal spray, they have only the supersaturated BCC solid solution []. Cold-sprayed AlFeNiCoCr alloy retains the same BCC structure as was observed in the powder []. In contrast, in the plasma-sprayed coating of the same composition, the FCC phase is observed as the major one []. Despite high heating and cooling rates, which prevent the elements’ diffusion development, factors such as high temperature, high oxygen concentration, and high specific surface of the powder inevitably lead to in-flight oxidation. cited_evidence.text: In this study, the powder milled for 10 h was chosen as a feedstock to deposit the coating by atmospheric plasma spraying. Prior to spraying, the feedstock powder was dried in an oven at 200 °C for 3 h to remove the moisture and improve its flowability. First, 316 stainless steel cylindrical specimens with dimensions of Φ 25 × 7 mm were used as substrates. Before spraying, the substrates were cleaned with an ultrasonic cleaner in acetone for 10 min, and then dried with a dryer. To improve the bonding strength of the coating, sand blasting one side of the substrate was carried out to obtain a certain cleanliness and roughness. During sand blasting, an Al2O3 particle with a size of less than 1.25 mm was used as an abrasive. The substrates were sandblasted under a compressed air pressure of about 0.5 MPa for 30 s. An APS system (3710, PRAXAIR SURFACE TECHNOLOGIES, Indianapolis, IN, USA) with a high-energy plasma gun (SG-100) was employed to deposit the coating. During spraying, argon was used as a primary gas, and nitrogen was used as a secondary gas, whose pressures were 0.4 and 0.3 MPa, respectively.
